questions.prompt: A composable re-executes on every frame of an animation happening elsewhere on the screen. What do you look at first?
options: Whether the list items are missing a key.
Whether the Compose compiler plugin is enabled.
Whether you can wrap more of it in remember.
Whether it reads a State it doesn't actually need — reading state is what scopes recomposition.
questions.explanation: Compose recomposes the smallest scope that read a changed state. If a composable is recomposing too often, it's almost always reading something too high up — an animation value, or a whole ViewModel state object where it needed one field. Sprinkling remember treats the symptom and hides the cause.

questions.prompt: State survives recomposition fine but resets every time the device rotates. What's wrong?
options: The composable is missing a key.
It's in remember, which doesn't survive configuration change — it needs rememberSaveable, or to live in the ViewModel.
Nothing — Compose state is not meant to survive rotation.
Configuration changes should be disabled in the manifest.
questions.explanation: remember survives recomposition; rememberSaveable survives process-level recreation by writing to the saved-instance bundle. Anything bigger than a scroll position or a toggle belongs in the ViewModel instead. Locking rotation in the manifest is the answer that gets a follow-up question you won't enjoy.

questions.prompt: This screen janks badly and sometimes hammers the API.
options: items() is missing its key parameter.
A side effect in the composable body — it runs on every recomposition, and it blocks the frame while it does.
questions.explanation: A composable body can run many times per frame and must stay pure. Loading belongs in a LaunchedEffect, or better, in a ViewModel the screen collects from. The missing key is a real second finding worth mentioning — without it, LazyColumn reuses the wrong items when the list changes.

questions.prompt: A Compose screen starts a network request directly in the composable body. What can go wrong?
options: Recomposition can trigger the side effect repeatedly; launch it from a lifecycle-aware effect or, preferably, state ownership such as a ViewModel.
Composable functions cannot call Kotlin functions.
Compose automatically caches every network response.
The request must run on the main thread.
questions.explanation: Composable bodies may execute many times and must be safe to re-run. Side effects need explicit lifecycle semantics through effect APIs or a state holder that survives and governs the work.
